item.title: Diverse Celebrations in February
item.description:
February Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diversity holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal awareness and help create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that there are many, and we, unfortunately, are unable to list them all.

Black History Month celebrates the history, culture, achievements and resilience of the Black community in the United States, despite the racism, violence and other systemic obstacles Black people have had to overcome since the country was founded. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Black History Month

  • BLACK HISTORY MONTH - National Today

  • Black History Month 2023: Facts, Origins & More | HISTORY

Events

  • Where to Celebrate Black History Month in Central Ohio
  • How to Honor Black History Month in Columbus
  • Libraries, museums and arts centers offer programs for Black History Month in Columbus

February 1 - National Freedom Day honors the signing of the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, which abolished slavery in America. This an annual observance celebrates freedom and those who fight to protect it. To learn more, click here.

February 5 - Lantern Festival is the first significant feast after the Chinese New Year. Participants enjoy watching paper lanterns illuminate the sky on the night of the event. To learn more, click here.

February 14 - St. Valentine's Day is a Western Christian feast day honoring one or two early saints named Valentinus. This holiday is typically associated with romantic love and celebrated by people expressing their love with gifts. To learn more, click here.

February 20 - Presidents Day is a federally recognized celebration in the United States that honors the birthdays of George Washington, Abraham Lincoln and every other U.S. president. To learn more, click here.

February 21 - Mardi Gras is the last day for Catholics to indulge before Ash Wednesday starts the sober weeks of fasting that accompany Lent. The term “Mardi Gras” is particularly associated with the carnival celebrations in New Orleans, Louisiana. To learn more, click here.

February 22 - Ash Wednesday is the first day of Lent on the Christian calendar. Its name is derived from the symbolic use of ashes to signify penitence. It follows immediately after the excesses of the two days of Carnival that take place in Northern Europe and parts of Latin America and the Caribbean. To learn more, click here.

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in December
item.description:
December Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diversity holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness and help us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that there are many and we, unfortunately, are unable to list them all.

December 1 - World AIDS Day is an international day dedicated to raising awareness of the AIDS pandemic caused by the spread of HIV infection and mourning those who have died from the disease. Government and health officials, non-governmental organizations and individuals around the world observe the day, often with education on AIDS prevention and control. To learn more, click here.

December 2 - International Day for the Abolition of Slavery is about raising awareness and reinforcing global efforts in combatting the scourge of modern slavery. Governments, organizations and individuals are entreated to take this day specifically as an opportunity to denounce the atrocities of slavery in its modern form that still exist in the world. To learn more, click here.

December 3 - International Day of Persons with Disabilities raises awareness of individuals with disabilities to improve their lives and provide them with equal opportunity. To learn more, click here.

December 10 - International Human Rights Day was established by the United Nations in 1948 to commemorate the anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. To learn more, click here.

December 18 - International Migrants Day reflects upon the challenges and difficulties faced by over 272 million migrants courageously building new lives in every corner of the world. The reality of migration is more than just starting over. Migrants travel in search of security and opportunities that will allow them to reinvent themselves. Others are escaping from discrimination and prejudice. Host societies need to evolve and welcome these communities for a better tomorrow. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • United Nations - International Migrants Day
  • History.com - United States Immigration Timeline

December 18 - December 26: Hanukkah is a Jewish holiday that is observed around the world for eight days and nights. It celebrates the victory of the Maccabees, or Israelites, over the Greek-Syrian ruler, Antiochus, approximately 2,200 years ago. To learn more, click here.

December 25 - Christmas Day is celebrated as both a sacred religious holiday and a worldwide cultural and commercial phenomenon. For two millennia, people around the world have been observing it with traditions and practices that are both religious and secular in nature. Christians celebrate Christmas Day as the anniversary of the birth of Jesus of Nazareth, a spiritual leader whose teachings form the basis of their religion. Popular customs include exchanging gifts, decorating Christmas trees, attending church, sharing meals with family and friends and, of course, waiting for Santa Claus to arrive. To learn more, click here.

December 26 - January 1:  Kwanzaa was created in 1966 by Maulana Ron Karenga. It is an African American and Pan-African holiday that celebrates history, values, family, community and culture. To learn more, click here.

December 31 - Watch Night or "Freedom's Eve commemorates the night of December 31, 1862, when enslaved and free African Americans gathered, many in secret, to ring in the new year and await news that the Emancipation Proclamation had taken effect. Today, Watch Night is an annual New Year’s Eve tradition that includes the memory of slavery and freedom, reflections on faith, and celebration of community and strength. To learn more, click here.

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in November
item.description:
November Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diversity holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness and help us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that there are many and we, unfortunately, are unable to list them all.

November 1 - 30, is National Native American Heritage and National Family Caregivers Month: 

National Native American Heritage Month celebrates the history and contributions of Native Americans. To learn more, click on the following links: 

  • National Native American Heritage Month
  • National Today – Native American Heritage Month
  • Native Americans: Tribes and Facts | HISTORY.com - HISTORY

National Family Caregivers Month, proclaimed in 2012 by former President Barack Obama, honors the more than 40 million caregivers across the country who support aging parents, ill spouses or other loved ones with disabilities who remain at home. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Mental Health America – National Family Caregivers Month
  • National Today – National Family Caregivers Month
  • Caregiver Action Network – National Family Caregivers Month

November 1 and 2 - Day of the Dead (Día de los Muertos) is perhaps the most colorful of November multicultural holidays. This Mexican holiday celebrates both life and death. It’s rooted in two traditions: the Christian observance of All Saints and All Souls Day as well as two Aztec festivals of souls of the dead. It includes vibrant costumes and tasty dishes. To learn more, click on the following links: 

  • Day of the Dead (Dia De Los Muertos)
  • What is the Day of the Dead holiday? An illustrated guide

November 11 - Veterans Day is a U.S. federal holiday honoring military veterans. The date is also celebrated as Armistice Day, or Remembrance Day, in other parts of the world and commemorates the ending of World War I in 1918. To learn more, click here and check out these links for upcoming events and celebrations:

  • National Veterans Memorial and Museum | Columbus, OH
  • 2022 Columbus Veterans Day Parade - 11/10
  • Columbus, OH Veterans Events | Eventbrite

November 13 - World Kindness Day is a global day that promotes the importance of being kind to each other, to yourself and to the world. The purpose of this day is to help everyone understand that compassion for others is what binds all of us together. To learn more, click here and check out the link below for more ways to celebrate:

  • 9 Ways to Celebrate World Kindness Day

November 19 - National Adoption Day is a collective effort to raise awareness of the more than 125,000 children waiting to be adopted from foster care in the United States. To learn more, click here. 

November 19 - International Men's Day emphasizes the important issues affecting males, including health issues that affect males, improving relations between genders, highlighting the importance of male role models and promoting gender equality. This holiday is celebrated in over 70 countries. To learn more, click here.

November 20 - Transgender Day of Remembrance was established in 1998 to memorialize those who have been killed as a result of transphobia and to raise awareness of the continued violence endured by the transgender community. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Transgender Day of Remembrance - Stonewall Columbus
  • Transgender Day of Remembrance | GLAAD

November 24 - Thanksgiving Day in the United States began as a day of giving thanks for the blessings of the harvest and of the preceding year. To learn more, click here.

To view a full list of Diversity holidays/celebrations/observances in November, click here.

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in October
item.description:
October Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diversity holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness and help us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that there are many and we, unfortunately, are unable to list them all.

October 1 - 31 is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, LGBTQ+ History Month, Global Diversity Awareness Month and Breast Cancer Awareness Month: 

National Disability Employment Awareness Month was launched in 1945 when Congress declared the first week in October as “National Employ the Physically Handicapped Week.” In 1998, the week was extended to a month and renamed. The annual event draws attention to employment barriers that still need to be addressed. To learn more, click here.

LGBTQ+ History Month is a U.S. observance that began in 1994 to recognize lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender history and the history of the gay-rights movement. To learn more, click here.

Global Diversity Awareness Month celebrates and increases awareness about the diversity of cultures and ethnicities, and the positive impact diversity can have on society. To learn more, click here.

Breast Cancer Awareness Month increases awareness of the disease and gets women the help they need. You can take part in Breast Cancer Awareness Month by visiting the National Breast Cancer Foundation (NBCF) and downloading their free Dense Breast Q&A Guide, making a one-time (or monthly) gift, or hosting a fundraiser to benefit the NBCF. To learn more, click here.

October 4-5 (sundown to sundown) - Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar, a day of atonement marked by fasting and ceremonial repentance. To learn more, click here.

October 10 - World Mental Health Day was first celebrated in 1993 and is meant to increase public awareness about the importance of mental health, mental health services and mental health workers worldwide.  To learn more, click here.

October 10 - Indigenous Peoples Day is an alternative celebration to Columbus Day and gives recognition to the indigenous populations affected by colonization. To learn more, click here.

October 11 - National Coming Out Day (U.S.) celebrates coming out for those who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender, and recognizes the 1987 march on Washington for gay and lesbian equality. To learn more, click here.

October 24 - Diwali is a festival of lights and one of the major festivals celebrated by Hindus, Jains and Sikhs. It symbolizes the symbolic victory of light over darkness, knowledge over ignorance and good over evil. To learn more, click here. 

October 31 - All Hallows’ Eve (Halloween), a celebration observed in a number of countries on the eve of the Western Christian feast of All Hallows’ Day. It begins the three-day observance of Allhallowtide, the time in the liturgical year dedicated to remembering the dead, including saints (hallows), martyrs, and all the faithful departed. To learn more, click here.

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in September
item.description:
September Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diversity holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness and help us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that there are many and we, unfortunately, are unable to list them all.

September 15 - October 15 celebrates Hispanic Heritage Month:

We celebrate the culture of the diverse community of people whose ancestors come from Spanish-speaking countries. Hispanic-Americans have been integral to the prosperity of the U.S., and they have left an indelible mark on our culture and economy. To learn more click here.

Below you will find valuable tools and resources which you can share with your staff, coworkers, family and friends.

Resources:

  • Timeline
  • Distinguishing Race and Ethnicity

  • Facts and Figures

  • How to Celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month as an Ally
  • 15 Festive Hispanic Heritage Month Activities
  • 83 Latinx-Owned Businesses to Shop Right Now and Always
  • Celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month with 25 recipes from Mexico, Puerto Rico, Spain and more

September 4-10 - National Suicide Prevention Week is an annual week-long campaign in the United States to inform and engage health professionals and the general public about suicide prevention and the warning signs of suicide. The campaign also strives to reduce the stigma surrounding the topic as well as encourage the pursuit of mental health assistance and support people who have attempted suicide. To learn more, click here.

September 6 - Labor Day in the United States. Labor Day honors the contribution that laborers have made to the country and is observed on the first Monday of September.  To learn more, click here.

September 11 - Ethiopian New Year is said to date back to the time when the Queen of Sheba returned from her visit to King Solomon in Jerusalem in 980 BC. The Queen was welcomed back in her country with plenty of jewels, also known as “enku” in the official national language. Enkutatash is the name for the Ethiopian New Year and means “gift of jewels” in the Amharic language. To learn more, click here.

September 16 - Mexican Independence Day or Dia de la Independencia tells the moving story about how Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla helped lead the fight to end 300 years of brutal class prejudice. His speech to the people of Mexico on September 16, 1810, marked the beginning of the decade-long fight for independence from Spain.

Today, it remains an important date to all Mexicans who celebrate it with fireworks, parties and parades. To learn more, click here.

September 18 - International Equal Pay Day, celebrated for the first time in September 2020, represents the longstanding efforts toward the achievement of equal pay for work of equal value. It further builds on the United Nations’ commitment to human rights and to stand against all forms of discrimination, including discrimination against women and girls.  To learn more, click here.

September 21 - International Day of Peace, sometimes officially known as World Peace Day, is a United Nations-sanctioned holiday observed annually on September 21. The UN General Assembly has declared this as a day devoted to strengthening the ideals of peace, through observing 24 hours of non-violence and cease-fire. To learn more, click here.

September 25-27 (sundown to sundown) - Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year celebration, means “Head of the Year.” It is a religious and festive holiday when family and friends gather together for meals and worship and grow closer to God. It is also a time for looking forward to a new year with anticipation and reflecting on the past year to improve ourselves for the next. To learn more, click here.

September 27 - World Tourism Day aims to foster awareness among the international community of the importance of tourism and its social, cultural, political and economic value. To learn more, click here.

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in August
item.description:
August Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diversity holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness and help us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that there are many and we, unfortunately, are unable to list them all.

August 7–8 (sundown to sundown): Ashura, an Islamic holiday marked by Muslims with a voluntary day of fasting, which commemorates the day Noah left the Ark and the day that Moses was saved from the Egyptians by God. For Shia Muslims specifically, this day honors the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali, who was the beloved grandson of the Holy Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). To learn more, click here.

August 9: International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples is observed on August 9 each year to promote and protect the rights of the world’s Indigenous population. Also known as World Tribal Day, this event recognizes the achievements and contributions that Indigenous people make to improve global issues such as environmental protection. 

Resources:

  • History of the Holiday
  • UNESCO - Indigenous Peoples Day
  • 2022 Virtual Commemoration
  • International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples - YouTube

August 15: Assumption of Blessed Virgin Mary, according to the beliefs of the Catholic Church, Eastern and Oriental Orthodoxy as well as parts of Anglicanism, commemorates the bodily taking up of the Virgin Mary into heaven at the end of her earthly life. To learn more, click here.

August 18–19: Krishna Janmashtami is a Hindu celebration of one of Lord Vishnu’s most powerful human incarnations, Krishna, the god of love and compassion. Celebrations include praying and fasting. To learn more, click here.

August 22: Hungry Ghost Festival is a Chinese holiday where street, market, and temple ceremonies take place to honor dead ancestors and appease other spirits. To learn more, click here.

August 23: International Day for the Remembrance of the Slave Trade and its Abolition and the anniversary of the uprising in Santo Domingo (today Haiti and the Dominican Republic) pay tribute to those who fought for freedom. To learn more, click here.

August 26: Women’s Equality Day commemorates the August 26, 1920, ratification of the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution that gave women the right to vote. Congresswoman Bella Abzug first introduced a proclamation for Women’s Equality Day in 1971. Since that time, every president has published a proclamation recognizing August 26 as Women’s Equality Day. To learn more, click here.

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in July
item.description:
July Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diverse holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness, which helps us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that we are, unfortunately, unable to list them all.

July 2, marks an important historical event in the United States – the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 which bans employers from discriminating based on race, religion, color, national origin or sex, and outlaws segregation in public places and schools. It was a historical achievement of the Civil Rights Movement, and one of the most important laws ever enacted in the United States.  To learn more, click here.

July 4: Independence Day (also known as the Fourth of July), a United States federal holiday that celebrates the adoption of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. The original 13 American colonies declared
independence from Britain and established themselves as a new nation known as the United States of America.  To learn more, click here.

July 11: World Population Day, an observance established in 1989 by the Governing Council of the United Nations Development Program. The annual event is designed to raise awareness of global population issues. To learn more, click here.

July 14: International Non-Binary People’s Day, aimed at raising awareness and organizing around the issues faced by non-binary people around the world while celebrating their contributions. To learn more, click on the following resources:  

  • About International Non-Binary People’s Day
  • 10 Ways To Step Up As An Ally To Non-Binary People
  • Ways You Can Be An Effective Ally

July 18: Nelson Mandela International Day, launched on July 18, 2009, in recognition of Nelson Mandela’s birthday via unanimous decision of the U.N. General Assembly.  It was inspired by a call Nelson Mandela made a year earlier for the next generation to take on the burden of leadership in addressing the world’s social injustices: “It is in your hands now.” It is more than a celebration of Mandela’s life and legacy; it is a global movement to honor his life’s work and to change the world for the better.  To learn more, click on the following resources: 

  • Nelson Mandela Day  
  • Nelson Mandela's Life Story

July 26: Disability Independence Day, celebrating the anniversary of the 1990 signing of the Americans with Disabilities Act.  To learn more, click here.

July 30: International Day of Friendship, proclaimed in 2011 by the U.N. General Assembly with the idea that friendship between peoples, countries, cultures and individuals can inspire peace efforts and build bridges between communities.  To learn more, click here.

To view a full list of Diversity holidays/celebrations/observances in July, click here.

item.title: The Office of Diversity and Inclusion Partners with the National LGBT Chamber of Commerce
item.description:
The Office of Diversity and Inclusion Partners with the National LGBT Chamber of Commerce

The City of Columbus, Mayor’s Office of Diversity and Inclusion is excited to announce the LGBT Business Enterprise Registration Program! As an LGBT Business, we are honored to work in partnership with you to grow your business and bring your dreams to fruition. As a certified LGBT business enterprise, we invite you to follow 4 EASY STEPS to establish a vendor profile with the City of Columbus and leverage the value of LGBTBE registration, which includes:

Vendor Listing in the City’s Online Directory - Increased Exposure - Connect with Key Decision Makers - Access City Contracting Opportunities - Attend Training Workshops and Conferences - Join a Network of Business Contacts and Build Connections

Step 1 - Vendor Portal Registration

Vendors must register on the Vendor Services portal before doing business with the City of Columbus and becoming LGBT Business Enterprise. To get registered, please visit the following link:

columbusvendorservices.powerappsportals.com

Step 2 - Contract Compliance Report (EBO Questionnaire)

After vendor registration, you will receive an email inviting you to complete the required Contract Compliance (EBO) Questionnaire. Vendors must be contract compliant in order to do business with the City of Columbus. To get compliant, please visit the following link:

columbusvendorservices.powerappsportals.com

Step 3 - LGBT-Owned Business Enterprise Certification

The NGLCC is the exclusive, third-party certification body that verifies that eligible businesses are majority-owned by LGBT individuals, and subsequently grants the Certified LGBT Business Enterprise (Certified LGBTBE) designation. To get certified with the NGLCC, please visit the following link:

nglcc.org/get-certified

Step 4 - LGBT Business Enterprise (LGBTBE) Registration

To register as an LGBTBE, complete our online registration in the City of Columbus diversity compliance system and provide a copy of your NGLCC approval/certification. To get started, please visit the following link: Columbus.DiversityCompliance.com.

For more information or questions, contact us at: DiversityCertifications@columbus.gov

Stay connected: columbus.gov/diversity

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in June
item.description:
June Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diverse holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness, which helps us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that we are, unfortunately, unable to list them all.

The City of Columbus Office of Diversity and Inclusion is proud to celebrate Pride Month. Learn more below.

June 1 - 30, is Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Pride Month and Immigrant Heritage Month: 

Pride Month was established to recognize the impact that LGBTQ+ individuals have had on the world, promote dignity, equal rights and self-affirmation, raise awareness of current issues and protest against discrimination and violence.

This annual celebration is commemorated with Pride parades, picnics, parties, memorials for those lost to hate crimes and HIV/AIDS, and other group gatherings. The last Sunday in June is LGBTQ+ Pride Day.  

Below you will find valuable tools and resources which you can share with your staff, co-workers, family and friends.

Resources:

  • History
  • Timeline
  • Facts and Figures
  • Terminology
  • Employee Discussion/Questions
  • 2022 Columbus Pride Events

Immigrant Heritage Month, established in June 2014, gives people across the United States an opportunity to annually explore their own heritage and celebrate the shared diversity that forms the unique story of America. It celebrates immigrants across the United States and their contributions to their local communities and economy.

Resources:

  • White House Proclamation on National Immigrant Heritage Month

  • About Us - I Am an Immigrant

  • #IAmAnImmigrant YouTube

  • What is Immigrant Heritage Month?

June 2 - Native American Citizenship Day, commemorating the day in 1924 when the U.S. Congress passed legislation recognizing the citizenship of Native Americans. To learn more, click here.

June 14 - Flag Day in the United States, observed to celebrate the history and symbolism of the American flag.  To learn more, click here.

June 19 - Juneteenth, also known as Freedom Day or Emancipation Day. On June 17, 2021 it became the eleventh American federal holiday. This celebration honors the day in 1865 when slaves in Texas and Louisiana finally heard they were free, two months after the end of the Civil War. June 19, therefore, became the day of emancipation for thousands of African-Americans.  To learn more, click here. To learn more about the Juneteenth Foundation, click here. To attend a Juneteenth event in Columbus, click here.

June 20 - Father’s Day is a holiday honoring fatherhood that is observed in different forms throughout the world.  To learn more, click here.

item.description:
May Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diverse holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness, which helps us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that we are, unfortunately, unable to list them all.

 

May is Asian Pacific American Heritage Month, Older Americans Month, Jewish American Heritage Month and Mental Health Awareness Month:

Asian Pacific American Heritage Month commemorates the immigration of the first Japanese to the United States on May 7, 1843, and to mark the anniversary of the completion of the transcontinental railroad on May 10, 1869. The majority of the workers who laid the tracks on the project were Chinese immigrants.

Below you will find valuable tools and resources which you can share with your staff, co-workers, family and friends to learn more about this important cultural group.

Resources:

  • History of AAPI Heritage Month
  • Defining Asia and the Pacific Islands
  • How You See Me
  • YouTube's Asian & Pacific Islander Creators and Artists

Older Americans Month was established in 1963 to honor the legacies and contributions of older Americans and to support them as they enter their next stage of life.

Resources:

  • OAM 2022 | ACL Administration for Community Living
  • Older Americans Month | Department of Aging (ohio.gov)
  • Central Ohio Area Agency on Aging (COAAA)
  • Older American's Month 2022 NY - YouTube

Jewish Americans Month recognizes the diverse contributions of the Jewish people to American culture.

Resources:

  • Jewish American Heritage Month (NMAJH)
  • White House Proclamation on Jewish American Heritage Month

Mental Health Awareness Month (or Mental Health Month), aims to raise awareness, educate the public and reduce the stigma that surrounds mental illnesses.

Resources:

  • NAMI.org - Get Involved
  • Mental Health Month | Mental Health America (mhanational.org)

National Minority Health Month (NMHM) originated with the 1915 establishment of National Negro Health Week by Booker T. Washington. In 2002, National Minority Health Month received support from the U.S. Congress with a concurrent resolution (H. Con. Res. 388) that “a National Minority Health and Health Disparities Month should be established to promote educational efforts on the health problems currently facing minorities and other health disparity populations.” The resolution encouraged “all health organizations and Americans to conduct appropriate programs and activities to promote healthfulness in minority and other health disparity communities.” NMHM helps to:

  • Build awareness about the disproportionate burden of premature death and illness in people from racial and ethnic minority groups.
  • Encourage action through health education, early detection and control of disease complications.

Resources:

April 10 - Ram Navami, a Hindu day of worship and celebration of the seventh avatar of Vishnu (Lord Rama). Devotees typically wear red and place extravagant flowers on the shrine of the god. For more information, click here.

April 15–April 23 - Passover, an eight-day Jewish holiday in commemoration of the emancipation of the Israelites from slavery in ancient Egypt. To learn more, click here.

 

April 17 - Easter is a significant date within Christianity and is the foundation of the Christian faith. Easter, also called Pascha or Resurrection Sunday, is a Christian holiday commemorating the resurrection of Jesus from the dead. Easter is inextricably tied to the Jewish tradition of Passover, one of the most sacred and widely observed holidays in Judaism. Passover commemorates the Jews’ liberation from slavery in Egypt and the “passing over” or sparing from destruction when the Lord “smote the land of Egypt.” To learn more, click here.

April 22 - Earth Day promotes world peace and sustainability of the planet. Events are held globally to show support of environmental protection of the Earth. For more information, click here.

item.title: Message from Mayor Ginther: Historic Investments in Neighborhood Safety
item.description:
Our city is at a crossroads. How we respond and recover from an unprecedented time in our history matters. We must make informed and forward-reaching decisions now to build the city we want to see in the future.

More than ever, we are collaborating with subject matter experts, established service providers and community stakeholders to incorporate new data and best practices to develop effective solutions to the many challenges we face as a community. Together, we will create  the safest, most inclusive and most resilient tomorrow,  for all our neighbors and all our neighborhoods, by learning from our past and being nimble, innovative and proactive today, and every day after.

My proposed 2022 operating budget includes historic investments in neighborhood safety that range from more police officers and firefighters to expanded programming across city departments – and to external partners, as well.

We remain mindful of the increase in separations among our sworn safety forces, especially in the Division of Police. My proposed operating budget includes more than $9 million for three new recruit classes in both Police and Fire, which will add a total of 170 new police officers and 125 new firefighters to our safety forces in the coming year.

Our newest police officers, in particular, will be trained extensively in community policing, which is crucial to bridging the divide between the community and law enforcement, and alleviating the current spike in crime.

At the same time, we are pursuing plans to expand police reserve units and support lateral moves from other agencies to further strengthen our public safety forces during a period of profound transition and demand.

Although our work requires that we keep a watchful and discerning eye on the future, we also recognize that we have an urgent duty to care for the officers we already have.

The 2022 operating budget will include new investments in wellness programs that connect first responders with clinicians who impart valuable skills, knowledge and resources – empowering our officers to thrive both on and off duty.

This is in addition to the planned police and fire joint wellness center, funding for which was part of our capital improvements budget approved by City Council last week.

Our commitment to holistic health and well-being extends to the broader community, as well. Key initiatives include:

  • Expanding the Alternative Response Program, which imbeds social workers and mental health professionals in 9-1-1 dispatch to facilitate more precise and robust emergency responses.
  • Expanding the city’s successful Safe Streets bike patrol to additional neighborhoods.
  • Expanding the city’s RREACT (Rapid Response Emergency Addiction Crisis Team) efforts, a first-of-its-kind initiative that provides follow-up services for opiate overdose patients.
  • Continuing TAPS (Teens and Police Service), a program that connects youth with police mentors.
  • Forming the Police Athletic League to promote healthy habits and physical activity while establishing trusting bonds between youth and public safety personnel.
  • Continuing cross-departmental responses to neighborhoods by coordinating city resources to create physical deterrents to crime.
  • Continuing investments in GVI (Group Violence Intervention) to advance strategies and resources that reduce violent crime.
  • Working with city departments and outside partners such as the Columbus Urban League for youth interventions, including PEP (Parent Enrichment Program), a collaboration with Columbus Urban League and Franklin County Municipal Courts to provide enrichment classes to families who have children on the cusp of entering the criminal justice system.
  • Continuing the work of the CARE Coalition and VOICE (Violence, Outreach, Intervention and Community Engagement), a hospital-based intervention program for victims of violent attacks.
  • Continuing investments in young people through My Brother’s Keeper as well as extensive programming in the city’s Recreation and Parks Department.

I am proud of the speed at which we have implemented some of the most sweeping policing reforms in our history:

We’ve changed the city’s use-of-force policy, implemented independent investigations into instances of deadly force, established the Civilian Police Review Board and Inspector General for the Division of Police, hired a police chief from outside the division for the first time in history to advocate for change, developed immersive, community-based training for new recruits, enhanced the body-worn camera program, and successfully negotiated historic changes to the F.O.P contract that will benefit both our residents and our officers.

Everyone has a role to play in building a safer, more resilient Columbus. We will not achieve our goals overnight. It will require time, patience, persistence and collaboration to see these plans through.

The challenges we face are complex, and they are varied – and so too are the solutions. But we are steadfast in our resolve to always do more, and do better, to achieve the greatest possible impact.

Columbus bands together, time and again, to meet the needs of the moment and to exemplify the exceptional standard to which other communities aspire. We have done it before, and we will do it again.

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in November
item.description:
November Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diversity holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness and help us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that there are many and we, unfortunately, are unable to list them all.

November 1 - 30, is National Native American Heritage and National Family Caregivers Month: 

National Native American Heritage Month celebrates the history and contributions of Native Americans. To learn more, click on the following links: 

  • National Native American Heritage Month
  • NATIONAL NATIVE AMERICAN HERITAGE MONTH -November 2021 - National Today
  • Native Americans: Tribes and Facts | HISTORY.com - HISTORY

National Family Caregivers Month, proclaimed in 2012 by former President Barack Obama, honors the more than 40 million caregivers across the country who support aging parents, ill spouses or other loved ones with disabilities who remain at home. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • National Family Caregivers Month | Mental Health America (mhanational.org)
  • NATIONAL FAMILY CAREGIVERS MONTH -November 2021 - National Today
  • National Family Caregivers Month - #CaregiverAnd | Caregiver Action Network
  • 2nd Annual Caring for the Caregiver Expo 2021 Tickets, Sat, Nov 6, 2021 at 9:00 AM | Eventbrite

November 1 - All Saints’ Day is a Christian holiday commemorating all known and unknown Christian saints. (In Eastern Christianity, the day is observed on the first Sunday after Pentecost.). To learn more, click on the following links:

  • All Saints Day: The history and traditions behind the holiday - CNN
  • ALL SAINTS' DAY - November 1, 2021 - National Today

November 1 and 2 - Day of the Dead (Día de los Muertos) is perhaps the most colorful of November multicultural holidays. This Mexican holiday celebrates both life and death. It’s rooted in two traditions: the Christian observance of All Saints and All Souls Day as well as two Aztec festivals of souls of the dead. It includes vibrant costumes and tasty dishes. To learn more, click on the following links: 

  • Day of the Dead (Dia De Los Muertos)
  • Dia de los Muertos | National Geographic Society

November 4 - Diwali is a Hindu holiday celebrated by millions of Hindus, Sikhs, and Jains worldwide. It’s a five-day festival of lights that may coincide with harvest and new year celebrations. Diwali celebrates different gods and goddesses, highlighting the triumph of good over evil and light over darkness. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Diwali - HISTORY
  • What is Diwali? All About the 2021 Festival of Lights (parade.com)
  • Diwali in History - History of Dipawali Festival, Diwalifestival.org

November 11 - Veterans Day is a U.S. federal holiday honoring military veterans. The date is also celebrated as Armistice Day, or Remembrance Day, in other parts of the world and commemorates the ending of World War I in 1918. To learn more, click here or check out these links for upcoming events and celebrations:

  • National Veterans Memorial and Museum | Columbus, OH (nationalvmm.org)
  • Veterans Day Parade (ohiomilvets.org) - 11/5
  • Columbus, OH Veterans Events | Eventbrite

November 13 - World Kindness Day is a global day that promotes the importance of being kind to each other, to yourself and to the world. The purpose of this day, is to help everyone understand that compassion for others is what binds all of us together.  To learn more, click here. 

November 16 - International Day of Tolerance was started by the UN General Assembly, with the goal of getting educational institutions and the general public to see tolerance as a staple of society, and it came after the United Nations declared a Year for Tolerance in 1995. This day is celebrated annually to help spread tolerance and raise awareness of any intolerance that may still be prevalent in the world. Although we should be tolerant every day, it’s always good to have one occasion to remind us just how important tolerance is. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • TOLERANCE DAY - Home
  • INTERNATIONAL DAY FOR TOLERANCE - November 16, 2021 - National Today

November 16 - Dutch American Heritage Day commemorates the longstanding friendship between the United States and the Netherlands. This holiday dates back to November 16, 1776, when the Netherlands was one of the first countries to recognize the United States as a sovereign nation. As a result, Congress declared a national holiday. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Dutch Americans - History, Modern era, The first Dutch settlers in America (everyculture.com)
  • Dutch American Heritage Day 2019 - YouTube

November 19 - International Men's Day emphasizes the important issues affecting males, including health issues that affect males, improving relations between genders, highlighting the importance of male role models and promoting gender equality. This holiday is celebrated in over 70 countries. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • International Men's Day – Men Leading by Example (internationalmensday.com)
  • International Men's Day 2020 - YouTube

November 20 - Transgender Day of Remembrance was established in 1998 to memorialize those who have been killed as a result of transphobia and to raise awareness of the continued violence endured by the transgender community. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Transgender Day of Remembrance - Stonewall Columbus
  • Transgender Day of Remembrance | GLAAD

November 25 - Thanksgiving Day in the United States began as a day of giving thanks for the blessing of the harvest and of the preceding year. To learn more, click here.

November 28 - December 6: Hanukkah is a Jewish holiday that is observed around the world for eight days and nights. Hanukkah celebrates the victory of the Maccabees, or Israelites, over the Greek-Syrian ruler, Antiochus, approximately 2,200 years ago. To learn more, click on the following links: 

  • Hanukkah - Chanukah 2021 - Menorah, Dreidels, Latkes, Recipes, Games and more (chabad.org)
  • HANUKKAH - November 28, 2021 - National Today

To view a full list of Diversity holidays/celebrations/observances in November, click here.

For more information about the Office of Diversity and Inclusion, click here.

For employees only, click here.

item.title: Diverse Celebrations in October
item.description:
October Diversity Celebrations

The world is rich with diversity, which is reflected in the observances celebrated by its various cultures and populations. Knowledge of diversity holidays and celebrations can enhance your personal knowledge and awareness and help us create a more inclusive and understanding workplace.

Stay tuned! Every month, the Office of Diversity and Inclusion will share information on different holidays, celebrations and observances. Please note that there are many and we, unfortunately, are unable to list them all.

October 1 - 31, is National Disability Employment Awareness, LGBT History, Global Diversity Awareness, National Italian American History, National Polish American Heritage and Breast Cancer Awareness Month: 

Global Diversity Awareness Month celebrates and increases awareness about the diversity of cultures and ethnicities, and the positive impact diversity can have on society. To learn more, click here.

National Disability Employment Awareness Month was launched in 1945 when Congress declared the first week in October as “National Employ the Physically Handicapped Week.” In 1998, the week was extended to a month and renamed. The annual event draws attention to employment barriers that still need to be addressed. To learn more, click here.

Below you will find valuable tools and resources that you can share with your staff, co-workers, family and friends.

Resources:

  • Timeline
  • Facts and Figures
  • Myth-Busting
  • Self-ID
  • Politics

LGBT History Month is a U.S. observance that began in 1994 to recognize lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender history and the history of the gay-rights movement. To learn more, click here.

National Italian American History Month honors the more than 26 million Italian Americans living in the United States. As the seventh-largest ethnic group, this month celebrates the unique cultural contributions they have made to the country. To learn more, click here and make sure to visit the The Columbus Italian Festival at St. John the Baptist Italian Catholic Church October 5 -10. 

National Polish American Heritage Month has been recognized since 1986. It was originally in August but changed to promote participation in schools. October also holds significance for Polish Americans as this is when Polish settlers first arrived in Jamestown, VA. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • POLISH AMERICAN HERITAGE MONTH --October 2021 | National Today
  • Polish American Museum | Current and Past Events
  • PAC (poloniacolumbus.org)

Breast Cancer Awareness Month increases awareness of the disease and gets women the help they need. You can take part in Breast Cancer Awareness Month by visiting the National Breast Cancer Foundation (NBCF) and downloading their free Dense Breast Q&A Guide, making a one-time (or monthly) gift, or hosting a fundraiser to benefit the NBCF. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Information, Awareness & Donations - National Breast Cancer Foundation
  • Pink Week: October 5-7, 2021 | Breast Cancer Resource Center (bcrcsb.org)

September 15 - October 15 - Hispanic Heritage Month recognizes the achievements and contributions of Hispanic American champions who have inspired others to achieve success. The observation began in 1968 as Hispanic Heritage Week under President Lyndon Johnson and was expanded by President Ronald Reagan in 1988 to cover a 30-day period. It was enacted into law on August 17, 1988. To learn more click here.

October 4 - St. Francis Day is also known as feast day for St. Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals and the environment, and celebrated by many Catholic denominations.  To learn more, click here.

October 6 - German American Heritage Day was first proclaimed by President Reagan in 1983. This date marked the 300th anniversary of the founding of Germantown. While research has shown that nearly all of the first 13 Quaker and Mennonite families who immigrated were Dutch (instead of German), this day has continued to be observed with German-themed activities. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • GERMAN-AMERICAN HERITAGE MONTH --October 2021 | National Today
  • German American Heritage Center & Museum (gahc.org)

October 6 - Birthday of Fannie Lou Hamer a grassroots civil rights activist in the 1950s and 1960s. She was one of the first Black Americans to register to vote after working in Mississippi for voting rights. She ran for Congress in 1964 – although unsuccessfully. On October 6, we celebrate Fannie as an activist who recognized that America’s vision of democracy was in great need of progress.  To learn more, click here. 

October 10 - World Mental Health Day was first celebrated in 1993 and is meant to increase public awareness about the importance of mental health, mental health services, and mental health workers worldwide.  To learn more, click on the following links: 

  • World Mental Health Day – World Mental Health Day
  • WORLD MENTAL HEALTH DAY - October 10, 2021 | National Today

October 11 - National Coming Out Day (U.S.) celebrates coming out for those who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender, and recognizes the 1987 march on Washington for gay and lesbian equality.  To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Celebrate National Coming Out Day with HRC! - HRC
  • NATIONAL COMING OUT DAY - October 11, 2021 | National Today

October 11 - Indigenous Peoples Day is an alternative celebration to Columbus Day and gives recognition to the indigenous populations affected by colonization. To learn more, click here.

October 20 - International Pronouns Day, seeks to make respecting, sharing, and educating about personal pronouns commonplace. Each year it is held on the third Wednesday of October. To learn more, click here.

October 21 - LGBTQ+ Spirit Day was created to demonstrate support for LGBTQ+ youth who face a disproportionate amount of harassment and speak out against bullying. Wear purple to show your support To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Join GLAAD this Spirit Day and Take the Pledge Against Bullying
  • Spirit Day - Stonewall Columbus

October 21 - Latina Women’s Equal Pay Day raises awareness about the wider-than-average pay gap between Latina women and white men. Latina women are paid 55 cents for every dollar paid to white men. To learn more, click on the following links:

  • Latina Equal Pay Day 2021 — Equal Pay Today!
  • Latina Equal Pay | Anchored by LCLAA for Equal Pay Today Coalition

To view a full list of Diversity holidays/celebrations/observances in October, click here.

For more information about the Office of Diversity and Inclusion, click here.

For employees only, click here.

item.title: Opportunities to Get Involved With the City
item.description:
Opportunities to Get Involved With the City

The Office of Diversity and Inclusion wanted to share two opportunities to get involved and share your voice:

  1. COVID-19's Economic Impact on Women: A Panel Discussion on the State of Women In Columbus, hosted by Columbus Women's Commission
  2. Police Officer Background Standards Review Focus Groups, hosted by Civil Service Commission

To learn more about each of these opportunities see below.

COVID-19's Economic Impact on Women: A Panel Discussion on the State of Women In Columbus

You're invited to join the Columbus Women's Commission for a two-part series examining the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on women.

The COVID-19 pandemic has been devastating for women in the workplace and has substantial implications for gender equality. Within the last year nearly 3 million women in the U.S. have left the labor force resulting in loss of pre-pandemic achievement gains made by women.

As the nation and companies look at economy recovery, what strategies are being considered to support women’s return to the workforce?

During the first webinar, Wednesday, September 29, 2021, Elyse Shaw of the Institute for Women’s Policy Research (IWPR) will provide a thorough overview of how the pandemic has affected women’s work experiences, economic security, and wellbeing. With local leaders, we will understand how women in our community have navigated the economic crisis, and what gaps persist.

This webinar is open to the public. Click here to register.

Part II- November- More details to come!

In the second webinar, we will examine practical tips and actions that individuals, employers and organizations can take to advance gender equity in the economic recovery. Attendees will develop an action plan with three practical actions to take in their own organizations and consider metrics to chart their progress.

This webinar is exclusive for the Columbus Commitment Adopter Network. If your employer has not signed the Columbus Commitment Pledge, click here for more information and for the opportunity to participate in resource sharing and learning sessions.

FEATURING

  • First Lady Shannon Ginther - Columbus Women's Commission Chair
  • Christie Angel - CWC Alumna, President and CEO, YWCA Columbus
  • Elaine Bryant - Cheif of POlice, City of Columbus
  • ELyse Shaw - Study Director, Institute for Women's Policy Research

Police Officer Background Standards Review Focus Groups

WE WANT, NEED AND WELCOME YOUR THOUGHTS AND OPINIONS! 

As part of the City of Columbus’s reimagining public safety efforts, we are wanting public input on what background standards are important and appropriate for those individuals selected for a Police Officer position.  Currently, these standards cover areas including honesty, family history, employment, criminal activity, illegal substances, and others previously determined important when evaluating potential Police Officer hires.

The current standards were developed and have been updated throughout the years with important public and stakeholder input.  However, it’s always good to ensure these standards remain relevant and appropriate so a complete review of the standards is being conducted beginning this month.

As you will see in the video below, the Civil Service Commission will be holding three focus group sessions, one each day on Tuesday, September 21st, Thursday, September 23rd, and Saturday, September 25th .  Seating is limited. So if you’re interested in being a part of this important work, please contact Wendy Brinnon at the Commission’s administrative offices at (614)645-7531 to confirm session times, locations, and available seating.  

Police Officer Background Standards Focus Groups 09/2021 - YouTube
